analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal capital gains tax entirely for individuals and estates.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from February 1995 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the tax code so that individuals, estates, and trusts pay no federal tax at all on capital gains — the profit from selling stocks, real estate, businesses, and other assets held longer than a year. It would also wipe out the existing smaller exclusions for gains on small-business stock and repeal the special 28% capital gains rate, replacing them with a zero rate. Capital gains are heavily concentrated among higher-income households, so eliminating the tax would chiefly benefit people with large investment portfolios, while the lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers or by borrowing. The bill was introduced on February 24, 1995, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and received no further action before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Individuals who realize capital gains — from selling stock, businesses, investment real estate, or other appreciated assets. Because capital gains are concentrated at the top of the income distribution, the largest dollar benefits would go to the wealthiest households. Fund investors, real estate investors, and owners of appreciated businesses would all pay zero tax on gains from 1995 onward.

how_it_helps.text: Allows a 100% deduction of net capital gain from gross income for any taxpayer other than a corporation, meaning no federal income tax on individuals' capital gains [S2][S3].
The deduction is allowed in computing adjusted gross income, so the gain is excluded before all income-based phaseouts and thresholds [S2][S3].
Applies to gains in taxable years ending after December 31, 1994, with a transitional rule capping tax on the remainder of 1995 gains at 28% [S3].
Repeals the 1993 50% exclusion for gains on certain small-business stock and the section 1(h) capital gains rate, replacing that structure with the full exclusion [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately other taxpayers. Every dollar of gain now untaxed is revenue that must be replaced by other taxes, by higher deficits, or by cuts to spending. Because the benefit scales with the size of appreciated portfolios, the tax burden shifts toward households whose income comes from wages.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the tax on capital gains removes revenue in proportion to how much gain is realized, and realized gains are heavily concentrated among high-income households, so the tax burden shifts toward ordinary wage earners or the deficit grows [S2][S3].

A zero rate on gains creates strong incentives to recharacterize ordinary income (wages, interest, fees) as capital gain, a tax-planning problem that has historically required elaborate anti-abuse rules — some of which this bill modifies rather than strengthens [S3].

The bill repeals the existing preferential treatment for small-business stock gains (the 50% exclusion added in 1993) and folds it into the broader exclusion, removing a targeted incentive for investment in new small companies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clean, simple zero rate on individual capital gains, which its supporters would argue removes a tax penalty on investment and risk-taking. The cost is a large, permanent revenue loss whose benefits flow overwhelmingly to households with large appreciated assets, while wage earners bear the offsetting burden. There is no provision to pay for the cut. The bill was never debated in committee, so its revenue cost was never scored in the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died quietly when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the bill on February 24, 1995, joined by Reps. Blute, McKeon, and Hancock as original cosponsors [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
Twelve Republicans cosponsored the bill in total; no Democrat did [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — the bill remained in committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers came out ahead in the narrow sense that no revenue loss was enacted; the wealthiest asset holders, who stood to gain the most from a zero capital gains rate, did not get the tax cut. Nothing stopped the bill except committee inaction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury; wealthy asset holders gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: All 13 supporters (the sponsor and 12 cosponsors) were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would show the full partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate tax on capital gains, and the largest realized gains belong to the wealthiest households. The revenue they would stop paying is revenue other taxpayers would carry.

industries.industry: Investment funds (mutual funds, REITs, partnerships, S corporations)
industries.note: The bill writes special pass-through rules so gains flowing through funds, REITs, partnerships, and S corporations also escape tax, benefiting the fund and real-estate investment complex and its investors.

The bill repeals the 1993 targeted 50% exclusion for small-business stock gains but replaces it with the full 100% exclusion, so these holders end up better off, though the targeted incentive is folded away.
